nodes.name: Rigid body core
nodes.purpose: Force, torque and impulse bookkeeping for a box-shaped chassis, plus the integration step that turns accumulated force into position and orientation

nodes.name: Car body and wheel contact
nodes.purpose: The arcade vehicle model: force accumulation, four wheel probes against track geometry, ground snapping, wall response, upright clamping, spin reactions and thrust/drag

nodes.name: Drive controller
nodes.purpose: Translates player or scripted input into a signed turn radius and a thrust value, owns the powerslide state machine and the recovery steer-back-to-route behaviour

nodes.name: Player input shaping
nodes.purpose: Ramps digital steering into an analogue value, converts throttle and brake into a drive signal, opens the powerslide on the drift button and arms the timed throttle-release boost

nodes.name: Racer physics and stats
nodes.purpose: Wraps the car body with per-racer stats, boost and curse state, per-surface grip recording from wheel hits and the route-following trajectory mode used by path-driven racers

nodes.name: Route trajectory playback
nodes.purpose: Time-parameterised playback along a recorded race route: playback speed ramps, lateral offset, tilt, jump arc and wall fallback for racers that do not drive themselves

nodes.name: Race camera controller
nodes.purpose: Third-person chase, cockpit and finish cameras with per-view profiles, exponential lag smoothing, turn lead, speed-driven distance changes and field-of-view shake

nodes.name: Brick pickups and powerup selection
nodes.purpose: Coloured pickup bricks, the white bricks that raise a held powerup level and the colour/level matrix that decides which effect fires

nodes.name: Powerup actions
nodes.purpose: Timed effect objects: turbo with three levels, shield with four levels, lobbed projectiles with a solved trajectory and homing projectiles

nodes.name: Racer versus racer contact
nodes.purpose: Impulse solution when two chassis touch, the shield-versus-shield rules that follow it, shove timers and the curse hand-over

nodes.name: Lap and checkpoint progress
nodes.purpose: Oriented checkpoint planes that count progress, the three-zone finish sequence that validates a completed lap and the standings comparison that follows it

nodes.name: Track hazards
nodes.purpose: Event-driven hazard objects: world-space trigger volumes carried by animated track pieces, with impact events fired at chosen animation frames

nodes.name: Race session loop
nodes.purpose: Frame pacing, the fixed simulation substep, the countdown that starts a race and the per-frame ordering of input, racer updates and camera updates

cards.name: Throttle, brake and turbo thrust
cards.summary: One thrust scalar per racer, doubled into a brake when the input fights the direction of travel, and replaced wholesale while a turbo runs
cards.behavior: At full forward input the controller hands the body a thrust of 54 units; any partial input scales that value linearly. When the requested direction opposes the current forward speed the same value is multiplied by 2 and treated as a brake, so lifting off and pulling back reverses more sharply than it accelerates. A scripted brake-to-stop path simply asks for twice full thrust in the opposite direction. Reverse while still pressing forward is halved to 0.5 so a stall does not fire the car backwards at full authority. A turbo ignores the throttle entirely and sets thrust to eight times full throttle, and while the car is scraping a wall the turbo is flagged as weakened and only half of that figure is applied. The value reaches the body through a setter that also recomputes the drag coefficient, so changing thrust immediately changes the terminal speed.

constants.name: fullThrottleThrust
constants.unit: thrust force units per update (fixed 40 ms simulation step)

constants.name: brakeThrustScale
constants.unit: multiplier applied to thrust while braking

constants.name: weakenedTurboThrustScale
constants.unit: multiplier over turbo thrust while touching a wall

cards.name: Steering as a requested turn radius
cards.summary: Stick position maps into curvature between a tight and a wide radius, softened at very low speed and clipped by the grip the tyres actually have
cards.behavior: Steering never sets a yaw rate directly. The shaped input is multiplied by the handling scale and then interpolated between an inverse radius of 0.025 and one of 0.00025, so a full deflection asks for the tightest arc the model allows, about 40 units, while small deflections ask for something close to a straight line. A radius larger than 4096 is treated as straight. Below a speed of 0.04 the requested radius is multiplied by 0.2 so a parked car cannot pivot on the spot. The physics layer clamps the request to the same 40 to 4096 band and the drive controller then compares the request against the minimum radius the current surface grip can support: if the request is tighter it is relaxed toward that limit and the wheels are put into a steering state whose gain rises as the requested radius tightens, using a slip ratio of 0.85 and a maximum facing offset of 0.7071 radians. When the tyres cannot support the turn at all the steering state is dropped instead. Handling from the car build enters as 0.003 per stat point plus a 0.7 base, so a strong handling stat tightens every requested radius.

constants.name: straightSteerSlipRatio
constants.unit: fraction of velocity lost along the slip direction

cards.name: Car build stat scaling
cards.summary: Three stat values scale handling, acceleration and top speed, and the boosted ceiling is a separate figure entirely
cards.behavior: Every chassis carries handling, acceleration and top-speed stats that default to 33. Handling becomes a multiplier of 0.003 per point plus 0.7, so the default sits just under 0.8 and the scale runs from 0.7 at zero to 0.85 at fifty. Acceleration and top speed share one shape: one minus a hundredth of the distance below 50, so the default keeps 0.983 of the base figure and only a stat of 50 leaves it untouched. Setting the top-speed stat also clears any running boost, which is what makes a garage change take effect immediately rather than after the current boost expires. Boost is not just extra force: entering one raises the speed ceiling from 120 to 176 and multiplies the recorded lateral grip by 1.5, so the car turns as well as it accelerates, and leaving the boost restores both figures. The vertical acceleration the whole model leans on is 39 units of acceleration, which sets how support, friction and drag forces read against body mass.

constants.name: statPenaltyScale
constants.unit: multiplier per stat point below the reference

constants.name: bodyGravity
constants.unit: world units per millisecond squared of acceleration

cards.name: Powerslide and release boost
cards.summary: A drift button turns four wheel probes into two axle probes, lifts the body, banks it and multiplies thrust on release
cards.behavior: A powerslide only opens when the car is not touching a wall, at least three wheels are grounded or it is already sliding, the travel direction still points within a cosine of 0.85 of the facing axis, and forward speed clears 0.05. Holding the drift button while turning enters the slide state, which switches ground detection from four wheel rays to two rays cast at the mid points of the front and rear axles, with a differently scaled sweep and a lift term added to the ray length. The body's visual bank angle is driven toward a target proportional to the inverse of the requested radius, clamped to 0.785 radians, moving at 0.005 radians per millisecond of simulation time. Steering while sliding uses the minimum radius the surface can support: the assist factor is one minus the ratio of requested to achievable radius, floored at 0.05, and the resulting gain and slip differ for a left and right handed slide. Releasing the drift clears the slide and the powerslide flags, and a separate release-boost flag, when it is set, multiplies thrust by 8 while it survives and expires after 300 ms, so a clean slide pays out as a short strong push rather than a permanent speed increase. At this commit the decompilation tests and clears that flag in the controller but does not visibly raise it, so the trigger itself is not yet matched to source.

constants.name: slideLiftRate
constants.unit: lift units per millisecond of simulation step

constants.name: slideSweepScale
constants.unit: sweep units per millisecond of simulation step

constants.name: slideBankRate
constants.unit: radians per millisecond of simulation step

constants.name: slideSteerSlipRatio
constants.unit: fraction of velocity lost along the slip direction

cards.name: Quadratic drag sets the top speed
cards.summary: The speed ceiling is enforced by a drag coefficient derived from mass, thrust and the ceiling itself, not by clamping velocity
cards.behavior: Whenever thrust or the speed ceiling is set, the body recomputes a drag coefficient as mass times thrust divided by the ceiling squared, and the drag force applied each step is that coefficient times speed, so the drag grows with the square of velocity and the equilibrium speed lands on the requested ceiling by construction. That is why the car accelerates hard from rest and then tapers: it is approaching a force balance, not a clamp. Rolling resistance from the surfaces under the wheels is summed over all four probes, scaled by a quarter and added to the same coefficient. Tyre scrub is applied separately: with steering or spinning active, a force of minus gravity times mass scale times surface friction times slip ratio acts along the velocity direction, and the remaining contact scale becomes one minus the slip ratio. Two more terms shape the low speed band, one proportional to lateral velocity and one that bleeds forward velocity when no throttle is held, both scaled by body mass. A resting body is finally snapped to exactly zero velocity once the integrated force is zero and the speed has fallen under a vanishing threshold.

constants.name: lateralScrubScale
constants.unit: mass-scaled force per speed unit per update

constants.name: coastBleedScale
constants.unit: mass-scaled force per speed unit per update

constants.name: rollingResistanceAverage
constants.unit: fraction of the summed wheel resistance

constants.name: surfaceForceShare
constants.unit: fraction of the summed per-wheel surface force

constants.name: boxInertiaFactor
constants.unit: inertia coefficient (one twelfth of mass times the summed squared extents)

constants.name: halfStepWeight
constants.unit: fraction of the acceleration term added to the position step

cards.name: Wheel rays and ground snapping
cards.summary: Four downward rays pick contact points, the deepest one snaps the body to the surface and the tilt of the contact patch becomes the support normal
cards.behavior: Each update casts one ray per wheel from just above the wheel position downward. The ray length is the elapsed milliseconds scaled by 0.04 while the car was already grounded, and zero on the first step after leaving the ground, so a car that lands probes at its own height instead of shooting rays through the floor. The best hit minus a padding of 0.4 defines the contact distance; every wheel whose hit is within that distance counts as touching and contributes its triangle normal to a summed support normal. With three or more wheels down the support normal is replaced by the body's own up axis and all four wheels are marked as contacting, which is what keeps the car stable on curved geometry. The body is then translated so the selected wheel ends up one ride height of 0.2 above its own contact point, and the wheel positions are recomputed. With no hit at all the car keeps falling and loses 0.008 of vertical velocity per step. A landing after more than 400 ms airborne is tested against the support normal: a downward impact beyond 0.05 rebounds, scaled by 1.15 with four wheels down and 1.3 otherwise, and cancels the contacts so the car bounces instead of sticking. Support force is gravity times mass scale projected along the normal, and each contact carries a share of one over the contact count plus 8.

constants.name: rideHeight
constants.unit: world units above the contact point

constants.name: wheelSweepScale
constants.unit: sweep units per millisecond of simulation step

constants.name: airborneDropStep
constants.unit: world units per update of vertical velocity

constants.name: landingAirborneWindow
constants.unit: milliseconds of airtime before a bounce is possible

constants.name: landingBounceThreshold
constants.unit: world units per update of impact speed

constants.name: landingBounceScale
constants.unit: multiplier on the reflected impact speed

constants.name: landingBounceScaleFourWheel
constants.unit: multiplier on the reflected impact speed with four wheels down

constants.name: contactForceDivisorOffset
constants.unit: added to the contact count before dividing gravity

cards.name: Per-surface grip, friction and support
cards.summary: Every surface triangle can override lateral grip, friction and the support threshold, and the wheels average them into the force model
cards.behavior: Track geometry carries a surface description per material, and each wheel hit copies four values out of it: a support threshold, a friction value, a lateral grip value and a rolling resistance, together with an optional constant force and a wheel particle. Missing values fall back to 3.0 for lateral grip, 0.25 for friction and 0.5 for the support threshold, so a plain surface still drives normally. Support force is only applied when its magnitude exceeds gravity times mass scale times the average threshold, which is how a loose surface makes the car sink or skate. Friction and lateral grip are averaged over the four probes and used in the scrub term and in the minimum-radius calculation, where lateral grip times gravity times mass scale is the centripetal budget and the radius is speed squared times mass over that budget. Entering and leaving a surface also fires events, and the paint on the surface changes the looping rolling sound, so a surface swap is audible before it is visible. Wheel particles only spawn above a forward speed of 0.008 and never while sliding, spinning or on a computer-driven car.

constants.name: defaultLateralGrip
constants.unit: grip units used in the centripetal budget

constants.name: defaultSupportThreshold
constants.unit: fraction of gravity required before support is applied

constants.name: wheelAverageDivisor
constants.unit: fraction applied to the summed wheel values

constants.name: fallbackTurnRadius
constants.unit: world units of turn radius when airborne

cards.name: Wall hits and body points
cards.summary: Body corner segments are swept against track geometry every step, and a hit rewinds the step, reflects velocity and kicks the nose off the wall
cards.behavior: Four body points are projected into world space and each is swept from its previous position to its current one against the track collider. The deepest hit wins, and the step is rewound to just before the impact: the remaining time is the elapsed milliseconds times the reported hit fraction minus 5, and anything under 5 ms is treated as fully consumed. The response removes the component of velocity going into the wall, then damps it twice more, taking 0.3 along the wall's horizontal normal and 0.15 of the vertical part, and adds a small push of 0.004 along the normal so the car separates. Vertical velocity is capped at 0.3 so a wall hit can never launch the car upward. If the wall normal opposes the body's right axis the nose is yawed away with an impulse of up to 0.004 plus a sign term for 200 ms, and any steering state is dropped on contact. The whole loop repeats after a rewind so a car pinned between two surfaces still resolves the rest of its step.

constants.name: wallHorizontalDamping
constants.unit: fraction of the into-wall speed removed

constants.name: wallVerticalDamping
constants.unit: fraction of the into-wall vertical speed removed

constants.name: wallPushoutScale
constants.unit: velocity units along the wall normal per update

constants.name: wallMaximumRiseSpeed
constants.unit: world units per update of upward velocity

cards.name: Upright clamp and visual bank
cards.summary: A pitch limit keeps the chassis from ever tipping past about forty five degrees, while a separate visual bank leans the body in slides
cards.behavior: After every integration step the body checks the forward axis: if its up component has fallen below 0.7071, meaning the chassis is pitched past roughly 45 degrees, the forward axis is rebuilt on a horizontal axis with the up component forced to the cosine of 0.7854 radians and the body is re-based on it. That clamps nose-dives and wheelies without touching velocity, so a hard landing or an explosion can rotate the car visibly but never leave it inverted or stuck on its roof. Separately the render-side bank target is chosen by state: a slide uses the negative of the sliding bank angle, a powerslide uses the inverse of the requested radius scaled by the tightest radius, by the slide factor and by the ratio of current speed to the speed ceiling, clamped to 0.785 radians, and any other state returns to level. The clamped target is then approached with a rate limited smoothing, so the lean reads as weight transfer rather than a snap.

constants.name: minimumUprightCosine
constants.unit: cosine of the forward axis above the horizontal plane

cards.name: Spin reactions and spin-out
cards.summary: Hits either spin the chassis for a counted number of turns or lock it into a timed, unsteerable spin-out
cards.behavior: A spin is expressed in turns and a rate, and is converted into a yaw impulse duration: the full turn time is one revolution divided by the rate and the impulse lasts that period times the turn count, so a two turn spin lasts twice as long. While spinning the steering state is cleared, the accumulated angular momentum along the body up axis is cancelled first so the spin starts from a known state, and the facing used for thrust is no longer produced from a requested turn radius, so nothing fights the rotation. A shield contact spins at 0.0089999996 radians per millisecond, which turns one revolution in roughly 700 ms, so a two turn hit holds the car for about 1.4 seconds; hazards spin at 0.01 and powerup hits at 0.007, so the same one or two turn reaction reads differently depending on what caused it. A spin-out is a separate, harsher state: it lasts 600 ms, makes the ground probe treat every step as a fresh landing, skips the per-wheel surface forces and blocks ordinary steering, and on the trajectory-driven path it also gives the car an upward jump of 50 units and drops its playback speed to 0.1, with a gravity of -100 pulling it back down and clearing the state at ground level. Ordinary driving can never spin the chassis; only hits, hazards and shield contacts can.

constants.name: routeSpinOutJumpVelocity
constants.unit: world units per second of vertical velocity

constants.name: routeSpinOutPlaybackSpeed
constants.unit: playback speed fraction of the normal route rate

cards.name: Car to car collision resolution
cards.summary: Racers exchange an impulse computed from relative velocity, contact offset and inverse inertia, then apply shield rules
cards.behavior: When two chassis touch, neither ghosted nor already spun out, the contacting car is pushed out of the other along the contact normal by the penetration depth. The impulse magnitude is the closing speed along the normal scaled by 1.75, which is a restitution of 0.75, divided by the sum of inverse masses plus the angular contribution at the contact point; each car then receives that impulse along the normal with opposite signs and light force feedback fires on both. The angular terms use each body's world inverse inertia at its centre of mass, so a hit on a corner rotates the car much more than a hit on the nose. Shield rules run after the impulse: a shielded car that is struck spins or shoves an unshielded opponent depending on its level, and a level one shield shoves only when the contact lies off the opponent's long axis, with the cosine of that axis under 0.7, using a 200 unit impulse that then acts as an external force for 750 ms. A shielded car also hands a curse over to an unshielded one instead of keeping it, and touching a cursed car transfers the curse to the other car. Computer-driven cars additionally receive a 750 ms speed ramp flag, and both cars take a 250 ms scrape-sound cooldown so a long contact does not machine gun the audio.

constants.name: shieldShoveConeCosine
constants.unit: cosine of the shove cone half angle

constants.name: shoveSlipRatio
constants.unit: fraction of velocity lost along the slip direction

cards.name: Chase camera follow
cards.summary: Camera sits on a pitch and height offset behind the car, leads into turns and lags behind both position and rotation
cards.behavior: The chase camera builds a flat view direction from the car's facing, then adds a look-ahead turn amount equal to forward speed times 80 divided by the requested turn radius, clamped to plus or minus 0.3 radians, smoothed at 0.00444 per millisecond so the lead eases in rather than snapping. The resulting angle is compared against the current view angle and only corrected once the error escapes a 0.014 radian dead zone, using an exponential amount of one over the view rate times elapsed plus one with the rate at 0.0167 per millisecond. The camera then sits at the follow distance of the active view profile, offset by that profile's pitch and height sines, and the whole transform is smoothed with the same exponential form for position and for quaternion rotation, which is what makes the camera glide instead of sticking to the car. Turbo changes the distance briefly: levels zero, one and two pull the camera 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 of the follow distance closer, while the top level just keeps the standard distance, and the scale eases back at a brick-settling rate. A cockpit mode attaches the camera directly to the car axes and a look-back mode mirrors it about the car.

constants.name: turnLookAheadScale
constants.unit: lead angle per unit of speed over radius

cards.name: Speed shake and view transitions
cards.summary: Field of view is shaken on a cosine ramp for half a second, and profile changes are cross faded instead of cut
cards.behavior: A short-lived field-of-view wobble provides speed feedback. When the shake window has expired the camera re-arms it for 500 ms and records the base field of view; on a car flagged as boosting it then picks a random offset that keeps the field of view inside a band from 40 to 80 degrees, either pulling away from the ceiling or pushing off the floor, and otherwise it uses half the difference between the base and the target field of view. The offset is read out as a cosine of the remaining time scaled by 0.02, by 0.1 and by pi, so the wobble is a smooth lobe rather than jitter, and the projection is marked dirty on every frame it runs. The finish camera blends over a 2000 ms window, mixing follow distance, pitch and height sine from the previous profile into the new one and sweeping a side offset round at 0.00157 radians per millisecond, so a switch to the victory angle orbits instead of popping. Audio listener position, velocity and basis are refreshed from the same camera object each frame, so the mix follows the view.

cards.name: Turbo levels
cards.summary: Three turbo levels differ by how long the boost runs, not by how strong it starts
cards.behavior: A turbo is a state machine rather than a plain timer. Activating one allocates its effect entities, cancels any turbo already running on the car, and takes a level from zero to two. The ignite phase lasts 400 ms while the model plays its first animation part, then the boosting phase runs for the level's duration, and finally a 700 ms fade plays before the effect is torn down. Each activation also applies a negative pitch impulse of 0.0025 for 125 ms on the lowest level and 250 ms otherwise, so the chassis pitches visibly as the boost starts. Boost duration is the only number that scales with level: about one second, one and a half seconds and five seconds. A special fly cheat keeps the top level boosting indefinitely. The physics side of the turbo is a thrust override, a raised speed ceiling and a grip bonus, and the camera separately pulls in behind the car for the first three levels.

constants.name: pitchImpulseRate
constants.unit: radians per millisecond of applied pitch impulse

cards.name: Shield levels
cards.summary: Four shield strengths from four to ten seconds, each with its own model, sound and contact reaction
cards.behavior: A shield is a timed aura with four levels. Activation first cancels any shield already on the car, then sets a timer from four seconds on the lowest level up through six and eight to ten seconds on the highest, starts a level-specific looping sound, and puts an outer and an inner shell around the car that follow its position and orientation with the up direction forced to world up. When the timer expires the state moves to a one second fade in which the alpha override is driven from the remaining milliseconds, and the shield is then removed with its end sound played five units above the car. The level decides the contact reaction: level one only shoves, level two adds a single turn spin, level three a double turn spin. Shielding also strips a curse from the car it is applied to, absorbs reaction hits without a penalty, and a level two or better shield returns a lobbed projectile to whoever fired it.

cards.name: Lobbed projectile solve
cards.summary: The lobbed projectile is given a flight time from distance over speed, then a vertical velocity that lands it on the predicted target
cards.behavior: Firing a lobbed projectile first finds a target point, or takes the car's own heading when no target is chosen, then predicts where the target will be by advancing it along its current velocity for the flight time. Flight time is horizontal distance divided by projectile speed, and the speed is nudged upward by the component of the shooter's own velocity pointing at the target, so firing while moving carries momentum into the shot. The trajectory solver then takes horizontal velocity from the delta over that duration and sets the vertical velocity to the height difference over the distance times speed, minus half of gravity times the distance over speed. That makes the arc land on the named target without integrating gravity error, which is why the shot reads as aimed rather than thrown. Each update re-evaluates position in closed form, horizontal travel being velocity times elapsed and the vertical term adding half of gravity times elapsed squared, so the flight is fully determined at launch. The projectile sweeps a segment against the world every step, expires when its lifetime runs out, and a shot that strikes a shield of level two or above is deflected back at whoever originally fired it, while an unshielded victim plays a hit reaction and drops a carried white brick.

constants.name: aimHeightOffset
constants.unit: world units above the target origin

constants.name: gravityHalfFactor
constants.unit: multiplier on gravity times elapsed squared

cards.name: Homing missile pursuit
cards.summary: Missiles lock onto a racer in a cone, then follow the checkpoint chain until the target is close enough to chase directly
cards.behavior: A homing projectile acquires a target inside a cone, refreshed at most once a second, and refuses to consider its own owner, ghosts, shielded cars or cars already spun out. While the target is far away the missile does not fly straight at it: it walks the checkpoint chain from the owner's current checkpoint, skipping checkpoints whose plane it has already passed, and steers at a ground point found by probing 50 units down from the chosen checkpoint and lifting the resulting hit by 6. That keeps missiles roughly inside the track even when the target is around a corner. Once the target comes within the square root of 3600 units the missile switches to direct pursuit, keeps its speed and aims at a point five units above the car, and a square distance under 9 counts as a direct hit. A ground probe ahead of the missile keeps it from sinking into the floor, limiting descent to 6 units per second, and a growing spiral offset of 6 per second gives the path a visible wobble.

cards.name: Brick pickups and powerup levels
cards.summary: A coloured brick selects a powerup family, white bricks raise the level, and only four families exist
cards.behavior: Pickups are ordinary bricks lying on the track that grow from zero scale over 400 ms, settle back to 0.8 scale, and become touchable half a second later. Touching one while the car holds no brick starts a 250 ms transition, then the brick respawns after 3000 ms; touching one while a brick is already held swaps the colours instead and leaves that brick active, which is how a player trades a family for another. A ghost car cannot collect at all, and a car that has already touched a brick in this pass is not offered the same one twice. The colour of the held brick chooses the family: red gives a lobbed shot, a grappling hook, a lightning strike and homing missiles as the level rises; yellow gives an oil slick, thrown dynamite, a magnet and a curse; blue gives shields; green gives turbo, with the top green level instead warping the car forward along the track. The level index comes from how many white bricks the car is carrying, capped at three, and firing consumes the held brick and returns every white brick, so charging is a deliberate detour.

cards.name: Lap validation and checkpoint progress
cards.summary: A lap only counts when the car passes through three ordered zones, and progress is a checkpoint count plus a fraction
cards.behavior: Track progress is measured on an oriented graph of checkpoint planes, each carrying a position, a plane normal and a fraction of the lap. A crossing is compared against the normal of the surface the car actually crossed, which resolves the direction of travel: a forward crossing of the lap boundary increments the checkpoint count unless the car is still flagged as having gone backwards, and a reversed crossing at the boundary zeroes the zone history and flags the car so that the next ordinary checkpoint pays the count back. Progress for standings is then the checkpoint count plus the fraction of the plane the car is heading for, so two cars between the same checkpoints are separated smoothly instead of sharing a rank. The finish line itself is handled by three overlapping zones: open track, the line zone and a post-line zone. A lap increments only when the car arrives at the line having come through the post-line zone with the line zone before it, so reversing across the line, cutting out and back, or parking on it cannot bank laps. When a car reaches the lap count the session marks it finished, awards cup points if a cup is running and switches that player's camera to the victory view. A countdown of 3000 ms precedes the race, and a car that is behind on time with laps still to run shows the gap for 2000 ms.

cards.name: Recorded route playback
cards.summary: Path-driven racers advance along a recorded trajectory at a scaled playback speed with ramps, lateral drift and a jump arc
cards.behavior: Some cars do not simulate forces at all; they advance a cursor along a recorded route. Playback speed is a scalar where 1.0 means the recorded timing, driven toward a target with separate acceleration and deceleration rates, with faster rates available while a boost or an external push is active. During the first two seconds of a boost the target ramps from 1.7 up to 2.75, and ending the boost returns it to 1. A curse drops the target to 0.5 and a ghost mode sets 4.5. Impulse-driven speed changes are clamped between -0.5 and 2.75, so a car can be pushed slightly backwards along its own route but never far. A lateral offset from the centre of the path decays back to zero at a fixed rate, and the slide state bends the path visually by sampling the route half a second ahead and comparing right axes, which gives cornering lean without any steering. Route jumps are a small ballistic arc under a gravity of -100 that clears the spin-out state when the car lands. Wall contact simply reverses playback slightly and rewinds the step, and large directional impulses from hits are converted into playback changes capped at 240 units.

cards.name: Analogue shaped steering input
cards.summary: Digital left and right keys ramp a virtual stick at a fixed rate, and the drift button changes both the rate and the return
cards.behavior: Input is not passed straight to the car. The player layer keeps a virtual steering value between minus one and one and moves it toward the requested direction every millisecond: 1.25 per second when a direction key is held, 8.25 per second when the value has to come back through zero to the other side, and 5 or 16 per second while drifting, the faster figure used while sliding one way and the slower the other. With no input the value decays at the idle rate of 2.5 per second. Holding both directions, or centring the value, pins the limits so the value cannot cross zero by accident. An analogue axis overrides the key ramp: its deflection sets the limit while the same ramp smooths the approach. The resulting value is multiplied by the car handling scale and handed to the drive controller as a curvature request, which is why keyboard steering on this engine feels progressive instead of binary.

cards.name: Pre-start boost window
cards.summary: A 100 ms turbo window opens at the lights and is consumed by a throttle press that lands inside it
cards.behavior: The boost window is a small state machine that only arms around the start of a race. A throttle hold longer than 2000 ms while the pre-start flag is still set opens a window of 100 ms and resets the hold timer. At the start the session asks every player's controls to make one attempt: if a window is still open it fires the green family straight away, choosing the strongest level when at least 60 ms remain and the weakest otherwise, and clears the window; if no window is open and the brake is not held it arms a fresh window of the same length. Because the attempt clears the pre-start flag, a long hold later in the race cannot re-arm anything, but any throttle press that lands while a window is still open runs the same attempt and also spawns a puff of smoke from the car. In practice that makes the start a timing test on a 100 ms window: a press in the first 40 ms of it pays the strongest level, a press in the last 60 ms pays the weakest, and a player who never has a window open gets nothing.

cards.name: Animated obstacle with impact windows
cards.summary: A moving crane carries a trigger sphere, and its swing only damages racers during two windows of its animation
cards.behavior: Hazard objects are loaded per track and activated by event ids from the event table, so a track can switch a hazard on and off as the race passes through it. This one rides an animated track piece: every update the entity's local origin is transformed up through its parent chain, scaled by the model and entity scale, converted to world space and handed to a trigger body whose radius is 3, so the collision volume follows the animation exactly rather than being baked into geometry. Damage is not fired on contact but on animation frames: a pending flag is set while the part time sits between 60 and 120 ms or between 210 and 270 ms, and the actual impact event fires when the part time then passes the 0 and 30 ms window or the 150 to 180 ms window, after which the flag has to rearm. That means the visual swing telegraphs the hit a fraction of a second before the trigger becomes live. A looping sound is anchored to the moving crane with a maximum audible distance of 300 units, and the update also keeps a projected shadow decal under it, so the player can read the swing from a distance.

cards.name: Frame pacing and fixed substep
cards.summary: The frame delta is capped, then sliced into 40 ms simulation steps that drive racers and cameras together
cards.behavior: The application clamps the measured frame delta to 100 ms so a stall cannot teleport the world, and sleeps to enforce a floor of 12 ms, which caps the frame rate near 83 Hz. The race session takes that delta and slices it: while time remains it takes a step of at most 40 ms and runs racer physics and every camera with that step, so the simulation advances at 25 Hz regardless of frame rate while rendering still runs at frame rate. Input shaping, force feedback and the demo text timer run once per frame before the slicing. Inside a step the order is fixed and observable: drive control for each racer, then physics for each racer, then drift lean, then roster bookkeeping, then car animation, then engine and spatial sounds, then timers, then standings. Hazards, event tables, particle animations, decals and audio all advance on the unsliced frame delta before the loop, which is why particles stay smooth while the physics marches in discrete steps. The countdown state holds until 3000 ms have elapsed, then starts the race, asks every player's controls to make a boost attempt and switches the music, which is the one place input is sampled on a state boundary rather than per step.
